cards.title: Bottleneck communication versus streaming space
cards.formal: Separate low-bottleneck distributed computation from low-memory streaming computation of the same function family, without imposing secrecy on the distributed protocol. The source asks for functions with low per-party communication that cannot be computed with low streaming memory. It does not specify the asymptotic separation, the allowed number of streaming passes or the input-order quantifier, so this is a research question requiring specification rather than a completed mathematical proposition.
cards.why: Asks whether distributing intermediate state across a communication network permits computations beyond those captured by a small sequential streaming state. A precise separation would clarify what per-party communication measures beyond the memory-times-passes simulation.
cards.status_note: The nonsecure communication definition and qualitative question were checked in the conference and full author versions. Later searches through 12 September 2026 and the 2025 security-dependent lower-bound report did not recover a precise pass/order/separation target. Current openness cannot be certified for an unspecified comparison.

sentences: Bottleneck complexity charges the largest expected communication load of any participant.
A small-memory streaming algorithm with few passes gives a low-bottleneck distributed protocol.
The source asks for a function with small bottleneck but large streaming memory, without secrecy requirements.
Its passage does not fix the pass budget, input-order convention or quantitative gap.
The card records those missing choices and distinguishes subsequent private-MPC lower bounds.

cards.definitions:
For n parties P₁,…,Pₙ, party Pᵢ initially holds only its own input block xᵢ, a string of k bits in the source’s illustrative setting. A function maps the ordered n-tuple of blocks to an output, with a single output bit at one party allowed in the source’s general discussion. This is the number-in-hand model; parties do not initially know one another’s blocks. The selected question does not require privacy, resistance to malicious behavior or cryptographic hardness assumptions.

Communication is synchronous and point to point. In round t, a party chooses its outgoing messages from its own input, random tape and previously received messages. Each message on an edge in a round uses a prefix-free code agreed by its endpoints. In particular, one cannot encode an arbitrary value for free through silence or a chosen waiting time. Let Cᵢ(π,x,r) be the total number of bits sent plus received by party i in protocol π on input tuple x and random tapes r. The source’s cost is BC(π)=max_i sup_x E_r[Cᵢ(π,x,r)]. The maximum is outside the expectation: this is not E_r[max_i Cᵢ], and it is not the sum of all parties’ loads. Its function-level cost minimizes this quantity over protocols that meet the required correctness convention. The source allows randomized protocols but does not fix a common error criterion in the streaming-separation passage. Its separate compiler assumes efficient next-message computation and a fixed communication pattern; those extra assumptions must not automatically be imposed on every protocol in this nonsecure comparison.

A streaming computation processes input blocks sequentially while retaining a bounded state between blocks. A pass is a complete traversal of the chosen stream; a multipass algorithm may traverse it again. The source observes that a p-pass algorithm whose communicated state has at most s bits gives a protocol of O(ps) per-party communication by passing that state around the corresponding chain or cycle. This statement uses the same input order and correctness convention in the two computations. It explains why both memory and pass count enter the comparison; a claim about memory alone does not fix the simulated communication cost.

To make the requested separation precise one must specify a family fₙ and the relation of k to n; an upper bound B(n,k) on distributed bottleneck; the allowed streaming order or quantifier over orders; a pass bound p(n,k); and a lower bound S(n,k) on streaming space with a stated asymptotic gap. One must also fix deterministic versus randomized correctness, how memory is bounded over random tapes, and any uniformity or explicit-construction requirement. The saved source does not make these choices. No particular polynomial gap, one-pass restriction, symmetric-function requirement or adversarial-order convention is certified by this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Pending a source-supported specification of the comparison. A complete result must exhibit the required function family and prove the distributed upper bound and streaming lower bound for precisely the same input and output task, with the stated order, pass, error and resource conventions. Until those parameters are fixed, a separation for one chosen interpretation is not a verified resolution of the saved question.

context_blocks.title: Per-party load is the comparison
context_blocks.text: The source separates the load on the busiest participant from total communication. It observes that computations can distribute their work over communication graphs with more structure than the chain or repeated cycle representing a streaming computation.

context_blocks.title: Streaming supplies one sufficient condition
context_blocks.text: Small memory and few passes give low bottleneck through transfer of the streaming state. The requested converse separation therefore depends on which stream orders and pass counts are allowed; the introduction states no precise quantitative version.

context_blocks.title: General bottleneck lower bounds answer another question
context_blocks.text: The source also gives an existential near-linear bottleneck lower bound for general functions. That shows that small bottleneck is not universal, whereas this card asks for a function that does have small bottleneck yet is hard for streaming.

context_blocks.title: Later lower bounds impose security
context_blocks.text: Eriguchi and Hiwatashi’s 2025 report studies perfectly private MPC, including correlated randomness and restrictions on communication patterns. Those hypotheses differ from the nonsecure computation comparison here and do not fix its missing streaming parameters.

cards.context:
The source separates the load on the busiest participant from total communication. It observes that computations can distribute their work over communication graphs with more structure than the chain or repeated cycle representing a streaming computation.

Small memory and few passes give low bottleneck through transfer of the streaming state. The requested converse separation therefore depends on which stream orders and pass counts are allowed; the introduction states no precise quantitative version.

The source also gives an existential near-linear bottleneck lower bound for general functions. That shows that small bottleneck is not universal, whereas this card asks for a function that does have small bottleneck yet is hard for streaming.

Eriguchi and Hiwatashi’s 2025 report studies perfectly private MPC, including correlated randomness and restrictions on communication patterns. Those hypotheses differ from the nonsecure computation comparison here and do not fix its missing streaming parameters.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
